Working with plans

From phoropter, commit 4ffb7d8. It describes the tool, so it’s the same on every site phoropter generates.

A plan is a short markdown file that records what you were thinking before a piece of work: what you decided, what you turned down, and what you guessed, each with its reason and where the reason came from. The code shows what was done. The plan shows why, in a form you can argue with later.

This guide is the format, in the present tense. Each rule names the plan that decided it, so the reasoning is there when you want it. Phoropter, the tool serving this page, reads plans written this way and links them to the code they're about.

An example

From mock-control, a plan about getting a library ready to publish:

## Decision: Selectors use the library's prefix, `mock-panel`
- where: `` scip-typescript npm @hypertheory-labs/mock-control . src/lib/panel/`mock-panel.ts`/MockPanel# ``
- quote: `selector: 'app-mock-panel',`

**Because (Jeff):** a rename is cheapest before the first publish. Breaking the class
apps is fine.

A heading says what kind of entry it is. The list says what code it's about, with a quote of the exact text as it was. The bold lead says where the reason came from. The quote no longer matches today, because this plan's own work renamed it, and phoropter shows both versions side by side.

1. Write the plan

Name it plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<name>.md. The date is the day you say "we're implementing this," and it's written only in the filename, so it can't disagree with a second copy. The name is any unique word that means nothing, so it can't turn into a category. (Decided in lanyard, aide's first plan, which defined the format.)

The frontmatter has base:, the commit you're deciding against. Then a # Title, and a short opening paragraph saying what the work is and why now, before any entries:

---
base: e92038c
---

# Get the library ready to publish

The class apps have used mock-control from inside the workspace. Before anyone installs
it from npm, its names and setup should be the ones we'd keep.

## Decision: …

Entries

Three kinds, each a ## heading:

  • ## Decision: <title>, then **Because (<source>):** and the reason in prose.
  • ## Decline: <title>, the same, for something you considered and didn't do. Only for alternatives someone actually raised. Never invent strawmen to look thorough.
  • ## Guess: <title>, then **Disproved if:** and what would show it wrong.

Reasons stay prose. A reason squeezed into a field gets shorter and worse. (lanyard)

Sources

Every reason says where it came from, in the parentheses: a person's name, measured, or Claude, not asked (or whichever agent). Combine them when that's the truth: Jeff and Claude, measured, then Claude, not asked. An agent told to do something won't ask why, so the record has to show when nobody said. A reason the agent guessed stays labeled that way until someone confirms it. (lanyard)

When a draft's open question went unanswered and its fallback became the decision, say so: Claude, unanswered, so its fallback. (phoropter: first used in the plans for links between plans, sorrel, and for source and date, marl)

Anchors

An entry can say what it's about, as a list under its heading:

  • - where: a file path, optionally narrowed with ›: a heading path in markdown (README.md › Setup › 1. Install), or a key path in JSON (package.json › version). Or a SCIP symbol, with the package version written as . so a release doesn't change it. Or another plan's entry: plans/<file>.md › <entry title>.
  • - quote: exact text from the file at the base, so a reader can tell which lines you meant. It's searched for only in the anchor's own file.
  • - where (new): something the work will create. No quote, since it doesn't exist yet.

Values go in code spans. When a value contains a backtick, use a double-backtick span: `a `b` c` breaks; `` a `b` c `` doesn't. (lanyard; the double-backtick rule is phoropter's, after awl, aide's plan on when as-builts freeze, wrote one wrong)

Anchor at the code as it is when you decide. The plan's own work will move it, and that isn't drift: drift is measured from where the work landed. (lanyard)

Keep a plan small enough for one person to review in one sitting. (lanyard, where it's still a guess)

2. Commit it before the work

That's how git shows the plan came first. From then on it's never edited. You don't revise what you believed; you write a new plan that links the old one. (lanyard)

3. Do the work, and depart from the plan when the code disagrees

Don't force a plan through code that doesn't share its understanding, and don't quietly do something else. Depart, and write it down in the as-built. Whether the departure was right is a later conversation. (lanyard)

4. Write the as-built

<plan>.as-built.md, beside the plan. Its frontmatter has head:, the commit where the work landed. Its anchors point at that commit, because they're about code the work made. (aide's grommet, the second version of as-builts)

Three kinds of entry:

  • ## Changed: <title>: the work departed from the plan. **Because (<source>):**
  • ## Chose: <title>: the plan left something open, and you decided it. **Because (<source>):**
  • ## Answered: <the guess's own title>: one of the plan's guesses, answered against its Disproved if. **Answer (<source>):**, then one of held, disproved, partly disproved, or not tested, then how much evidence that rests on.

Keep departures and choices apart. A reviewer wants the departures first, and Chose: is the comfortable label. (grommet; reading the verdict as structure is phoropter's burlap)

Anything else worth knowing, like a finding that isn't an answer to a guess, goes in the as-built's opening prose, not in an entry. (phoropter: burlap's as-built, which filed a finding as an answer first)

An as-built can say nothing changed. Nothing requires one, and nothing flags a missing one. (lanyard)

5. It freezes

An as-built is frozen once someone else could have read it, because from then on someone may have anchored to it, and it mustn't change underneath them. Before that, fix it freely. When that is depends on how your team shares work: a push, a pull request, a merge. If you're unsure, treat it as frozen once it's merged into your main line. Anything learned after that belongs in a new plan or a revisit. Phoropter can't tell when this happened and doesn't check; it's advice with a reason, not a rule it enforces. (aide's awl said "committed"; phoropter's twill, the plan that brought this guide here, made it "once someone else could have read it")

6. When an earlier plan's ground is wrong, revisit it

If the work runs into something an earlier plan decided or assumed, don't decide it inside the current plan; that re-decides the old plan in the wrong frame. Stop, and say so in the current as-built: ## Changed: "stopped here; revisiting …". Then write a revisit: a new plan with revisits: plans/<file>.md in its frontmatter, naming exactly one plan. It asks the question in that plan's frame, and every reason says what moved: the world, the code, or your understanding. The outcome can be "it still holds." Revisiting your own plan is the same move. (aide's bodkin, on revisits; phoropter's burlap is one, reversing quince's decision not to read verdicts)

Sometimes the earlier plan never wrote down what it assumed. Then the revisit anchors where the assumption shows, in the code or the docs, and says it wasn't in the plan. That records a gap in the old plan, which is worth knowing too. (mock-control's tallow, the first revisit, about MSW 3: "MSW 2" was a line in the README, never an entry in the plan it revisited)

To answer a guess from an earlier plan, restate it as a ## Guess: in your plan, anchored at the original, and answer it in your as-built. (mock-control's vellum, following its README in a fresh app, answered pumice's @source guess this way)

Drafts (optional)

When you're unsure, or the shared understanding looks thin, put the plan up as a draft before committing it, so someone can question it before it becomes testimony. The agent decides when. A draft can have no questions at all: "look, then tell me to go." Every open question carries its fallback, so "go" and silence both mean proceed, and only annotations change anything. It's never an approval gate.

Drafts are done by hand for now: the draft is a markdown file the person reads and annotates in their editor. Phoropter doesn't serve them yet. (phoropter: marl, on source and date, was the first)

Older plans

Plans are read as written. Plans from before a rule here existed may use earlier forms, like an as-built that uses Changed: for everything, or a cart: line. Phoropter shows them as they are and doesn't rewrite or flag them.

Squash merges and rebases

Plans record commits: base: and head:. A squash merge or a rebase replaces the work's commits with new ones, and the as-built was written before that happened, so its head: names a commit that isn't on your main line. Once the branch is deleted, that commit may be gone. Phoropter doesn't reconcile this today: when head: isn't a commit it can find, it shows the text as written, and the as-built's anchors are shown only at the generated commit. Plans read best on a history of meaningful commits that are merged, not squashed. (phoropter's twill; not yet seen in a real repository)

Reading the site

Every page says which repository and commit it was generated from. The home page lists plans oldest first and the places they anchor; each place lists the plans that touch it, newest first. The profile defines every link relation and microdata property, so an agent can read the same pages a person does.
